slides.name: Understanding 12-Leads, ECG Components, Artifacts& Lead Morphology COMPILED AND PRESENTED BY AO IDRIS Introduction to ECG Interpretation •Understand the concept of the 12-lead ECG and the Einthoven Triangle. •Recognize the key waves, segments, and intervals of a standard ECG. •Identify common ECG artifactsand their causes. •Understand normal lead morphology and what it tells us about the heart. Learning Objectives •Definition: A recording of the heart’s electrical activity from 12 different perspectives. •Includes 3 limb leads, 3 augmented limb leads, and 6 chest (precordial) leads. What is a 12-Lead ECG? •Named after Willem Einthoven, who invented the ECG. •Formed by leads I, II, and III across the limbs (RA, LA, LL). •Lead I: LA (+) to RA (−) •Lead II: LL (+) to RA (−) •Lead III: LL (+) to LA (−) The Einthoven Triangle •aVR: RA to heart center(the lead attached to right arm (-deflection). •aVL: LA to heart center(the lead attached to left arm (+ deflection). •aVF: LL to heart center(the lead attached to the left foot (+ deflection). a = augmented; V = voltage Chest leads: V1–V6: Chest leads placed from 4 th ICS to midaxillaryline on the 5 th ICS. Augmented Limb Leads & Chest Leads •ECG records electrical depolarization and repolarization. •Key components: P wave, QRS complex, T wave •Depolarization –electrical activation → muscle contraction. •Repolarization –return to resting state → muscle relaxation. •Systole = Contraction, Diastole = Relaxation The ECG Complex Overview P Wave •Atrial depolarization •Duration: < 0.12s, Amplitude: < 2.5mm in limb leads •Clinical Insight: Peaked P may indicate right atrial enlargement. QRS Complex •Ventricular depolarization •Duration: < 0.12s •Q wave: first negative deflection •R wave: first positive deflection •S wave: negative deflection after R •QRS wave amplitude greater than 5 mm or 0.5 mV is written in capital Letter e.g. Q, R and S. •QRS wave amplitude lesser than 5 mm or 0.5 mV is written in small letter e.g. q, r and s. T Wave and U wave •T wave: Ventricular repolarization •U wave (if present): U wave (+) is produced by depolarisation of the papillary muscles –an inconstant finding or electrolyte disturbance •Clinical Insight: Inverted T waves may suggest ischemia. Intervals and Segments •PR Interval: Atrial to ventricular conduction (0.12– 0.20s). •QT Interval: (about 0.40s) Total time for ventricular depolarization and repolarization (corrected = QTc) •ST Segment: Time between depolarization and repolarization. What are Artifacts? •Unwanted signals that can mimic or obscure cardiac activity. •Can lead to misinterpretation if not recognized. Common Types of Artifacts •Muscle Tremor: Irregular baseline from muscle activity. •Motion Artifact: Large spikes from patient movement. •60-cycle Interference: Uniform small waves from electrical interference. •Loose Electrode: Baseline wander or dropped signals. Reducing Artifacts •Ensure good electrode-skin contact. •Patient still and relaxed. •Avoid electrical devices near ECG. •Use alcohol wipes before placing electrodes. Understanding Lead Morphology •Different leads view the heart from different angles •Each lead has a characteristic waveform shape in a healthy heart •Lead I: Upright P, QRS, T •Lead II: Ideal for rhythm –upright P, QRS, T •aVR: Typically inverted waves •aVL: Small amplitude; QRS can be biphasic or upright. •aVF: Upright P, QRS, and T waves. Precordial Lead Progression •V1–V2: Mostly negative QRS •V3–V4: Transition zone •V5–V6: Mostly positive QRS •Clinical Insight: Poor R-wave progression may suggest anterior MI. Limb Lead Morphology Normal 12 lead ECG strip •12-lead ECG gives a complete electrical picture of the heart. •Key components: P wave, QRS complex, T wave, PR/QT intervals. •Recognizing artifactsis essential for accurate diagnosis. •Lead morphology varies and helps in locating abnormalities. Summary Why is lead II considered best for rhythm strip and determination of sinus rhythm? Question •Books: Rapid Interpretation of ECGsby Dale Dubin, ECG Made Easy by John Hampton. •Online simulators and ECG practice platforms (e.g., ECGpedia, Life in the Fast Lane, Google). References & Resources
